blurb_html: How sushi chefs shape nigiri, move by move: kote-gaeshi (the standard), tate-gaeshi (for slippery toppings) and hon-te-gaeshi (the old way) — which hand, which fingers, which way it turns.

intro_html: Nigiri is shaped with a fixed sequence of hand moves, and the sequences have names: te-gaeshi, “hand turns”. All of them start the same way (steps 1–8), then differ in how the piece is turned over. Kote-gaeshi is the one to learn first. Written for a right-handed cook: the left hand holds the fish and the piece, the right hand brings the rice and does most of the pressing. Start with sushi rice at about body temperature, and practise a few rice-only pieces.

notes.html:
TechniqueMoves (by source)DifficultyUsed for
小手返し kote-gaeshi — “small-hand turn”one roll-over + 4 squeezes (Ginza Watari); 2 shaping moves (Tencho); 9 photo stages (Yoshino-zushi)easiestthe standard today — most chefs, and where beginners start
縦返し tate-gaeshi — “vertical turn”hand-over flip + 4 edges (Ginza Watari); no formal countmediumtoppings that slide off the rice — tamago, octopus, boiled shrimp
本手返し hon-te-gaeshi — “main-hand turn”8 stages (Niizu); shaping “repeated 4 times” (Yoshino-zushi); ~5 after the basic shape (Ginza Watari)hardestthe oldest (Meiji era); a few traditional shops

The counts differ because sources split the same motion differently — some count prep and the wasabi, some only the presses, some count one round where others count two. Two more names exist, itte-gaeshi and yokote-gaeshi, but no source describes them step by step, so they’re not shown.

• Which fingers pinch the sides in kote-gaeshi: right thumb and middle (Ginza Watari, Tencho, Sushi University), right index and thumb (Niizu), or the left thumb with the right thumb and middle (Yoshino-zushi); Zojirushi shapes the sides with the left hand and only rests the right fingers on top.
  • Roll direction: most say forward over the fingertips; one says towards you, and some chefs roll the other way or flip with the left hand alone.
  • Tate-gaeshi: two sources describe standing the topping upright on the rice instead of the vertical flip.
  • The page follows the majority each time.

The kote-gaeshi roll's axis (step 10), how the piece turns in the tate-gaeshi flip (step 17) and how the wrists roll in hon-te-gaeshi (step 19) aren't described in any source read; the pictures show the most likely reading.

• About 18–20 g of rice per piece (15 g for a small one).
  • Before the Taisho era pieces were 2–4 times this size.

• Few movements, light pressure: the rice should hold on the way to the soy and come apart in the mouth.
  • Every extra press packs it denser.
Swap every hand: fish and piece in the right hand, rice and pressing with the left; turns go counter-clockwise.

• Buy fish sold for raw eating and keep it cold until you slice it.
  • Salmon for sushi should have been frozen first.
  • Eat nigiri the day it's made.

steps.body_html:
• Mix the cold water and rice vinegar in a small bowl.
  • Dip the right middle finger to the first joint and rub the water over both palms.
  • Clap off the excess — one hand a loose fist, one open. Damp, not wet: too much water and the rice falls apart.

how.caption: Middle finger into the tezu, to the first joint.
Rub it over both palms, then clap off the excess.

steps.title: Tezu: wet the hands

steps.body_html:
• Cut across the grain (the faint white lines).
  • Tilt the knife 30–45°, set the heel on the far edge and draw it towards you in one long pull — don't saw.
  • Slices about 7–8 cm long, 3 cm wide and 3–5 mm thick, about 14 g each.

how.caption: One long pull towards you, knife tilted 30–45°.

steps.title: Slice the fish

uses_rows.amount_html: ~200 g (16 slices)
uses_rows.name_html: Sashimi-grade tuna or salmon, a block (saku)

steps.body_html:
• Lay a slice across the inner side of the left fingers, one end near the finger roots — not in the middle of the palm.
  • The neat cut face goes down, against the fingers; the side that will get the wasabi faces up.
  • The rice will sit over the second and third joints of the fingers.
steps.title: Fish onto the left fingers

steps.body_html:
• With the right fingertips, take about 18–20 g of rice from the tub.
  • Round it loosely into an oblong in the cupped right fingers — no squeezing.

how.caption: Take the rice with the fingertips; round it loosely, don't squeeze.

steps.title: Take the rice (shari)

uses_rows.amount_html: ~300 g (18–20 g each)

steps.body_html: Still cradling the rice with the other right fingers, dab a pea of wasabi on the middle of the fish with the right index finger.
steps.title: Wasabi

steps.body_html:
• Set the rice on the fish. The left hand cups a little so the fish bends up to the rice.
  • The left thumb, raised slightly, flattens and spreads the rice over the fish.

how.caption: The left thumb spreads the rice over the fish.

steps.title: Rice onto the fish

steps.body_html:
• The left thumb pushes a small hollow into the middle of the rice, straight down.
  • It keeps air inside so the rice falls apart in the mouth: firm outside, airy inside.

how.caption: The thumb dent: straight down into the middle.

steps.title: The thumb dent

steps.body_html:
• The right index finger and thumb press the two short ends of the rice.
  • Then they press the long sides lightly — a rough rectangle.
  • Fish still underneath, rice on top, lying across the left fingers.

how.caption: Right thumb and index press the two short ends.

steps.title: Basic shape

steps.body_html: Curl the left fingertips up around the piece (still fish down, rice up); the right hand hovers lightly over the top.
steps.title: Enclose

steps.body_html:
• Open and straighten the left fingers: the piece rolls forward over the fingertips, away from you, and turns over — it ends fish up, back on the left fingers.
  • The right index finger and thumb catch it and guide it back down.
  • It rolls around its long side (inferred from where the next presses land — no source states the axis).

how.caption: Left fingers open: the piece rolls forward over the fingertips.
The right index and thumb catch it — fish up.

steps.title: Roll it over

steps.body_html: The right thumb and middle finger pinch the two long sides inward, wrapping the fish around the rice; the left hand cradles the piece.

how.caption: Right thumb and middle finger pinch the long sides.

steps.title: Squeeze the sides

steps.body_html:
• The left thumb presses the near short end square.
  • At the same time the right index and middle fingers rest on top of the fish like a lid — resting, not pushing down. The pressure comes from the left hand lifting into them.

images.alt: Square the end, cap the top

how.caption: Left thumb squares the end; right fingers rest on top like a lid.

steps.title: Square the end, cap the top

steps.body_html: The right index finger and thumb pick the piece up by its sides and turn it 180° clockwise (seen from above) on the left fingers, so the two ends swap.

how.caption: Turn it 180° clockwise on the left fingers.

steps.title: Half-turn

steps.body_html: Squeeze the long sides again (they loosen when the end is pressed), then press the other short end with the left thumb, the right fingertips only resting on top.
steps.title: Repeat

steps.body_html:
• The right thumb and index finger wrap the fish snugly over the rice at its middle.
  • Lift the piece by its sides with the right hand onto the plate. From the side it looks like a boat: the fish draped over, the bottom rounded.
steps.title: Finish

steps.body_html:
• After the basic shape (step 8), open the right thumb and index finger to the width of the piece.
  • Take hold of it by the edges where the fish meets the rice. Which pair of edges isn't stated in the sources.
steps.title: Right hand to the edges

steps.body_html:
• The left hand turns over, back of the hand up, laying the piece into the right hand.
  • The piece now stands upright, fish up, held between the right thumb and index finger — the “vertical” in the name. The topping is barely touched, which is the point.
  • Exactly how the piece itself rotates isn't described by any source.

how.caption: Tate-gaeshi: the left hand turns over into the right.
The piece stands upright, fish up, in the right hand.

steps.title: The hand-over flip

steps.body_html: Set it back on the left fingers as it is, fish up, and squeeze all four edges as in kote-gaeshi (steps 11–14).

images.alt: Back to the left hand, four edges

steps.title: Back to the left hand, four edges

steps.body_html:
• After the rice is on and flattened (step 6), the right index finger presses one short end.
  • The right index and middle fingers then take the piece onto the right hand, that end at the fingertips — the signature double turn.
  • How each wrist rolls isn't stated; the picture shows the left palm turning down over the right palm turning up (inferred).

how.caption: Hon-te-gaeshi: both hands turn over together.

steps.title: Both hands turn over together

steps.body_html:
• The left hand covers the piece from above and takes it back: the hands swap top and bottom.
  • The piece lies on the left palm again, rice up, the end you pressed now at the little-finger side.

how.caption: The left hand covers it and takes it back — rice up.

steps.title: Cover and swap

steps.body_html: Roll it forward over the left fingertips so the fish comes up (the kote-gaeshi roll), then press the long sides with the right index finger and thumb.
steps.title: Roll forward, press the sides

steps.body_html:
• The right index finger and thumb turn the piece 180° clockwise; squeeze the sides again.
  • A second clockwise half-turn, then close the whole hand lightly around it and a last gentle squeeze of the sides.
steps.title: Half-turns and finish

steps.body_html:
• Fish draped over the top with a little overhang, a rounded boat-shaped bottom, one bite.
  • Serve straight away with soy sauce and ginger. Dip the fish side, not the rice.
steps.title: Serve

timeline.note_html: Slice the fish in small batches and keep the rest of the block covered in the fridge. Work fast: warm hands warm the fish, and every extra movement packs the rice.
